audio.t: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Doctor Chen, one of the counselors at the Student Counseling Center. Since many of you have just finished your midterms, I'd like to talk about where you can get support this semester. First, every student can have up to eight free one-on-one sessions each academic year. Everything you share with us is confidential, which means we won't tell your professors or your parents without your permission, except in an emergency.

Second, if you prefer not to talk face to face, we now offer video sessions in the evening, and international students can request a counselor who speaks English. Third, we run small group workshops every week. This month, the topics are test anxiety and healthy sleep habits. Each group has only ten seats, so please sign up early through the student portal.
Finally, remember that you don't have to be in a crisis to visit us. Many students come simply because they feel a little lost. Asking for help early is a sign of strength, not weakness.

passage: In the two weeks after midterm exams, the university's Student Counseling Center received more than 300 appointment requests, almost twice the number from the same period last year. Director Lin Mei-hua says the increase is not necessarily bad news. "It shows that students are more willing to ask for help," she explained. "Ten years ago, many students felt ashamed to walk through our door."

Still, the rise in demand has created a problem: waiting time. Last month, some students had to wait up to two weeks for a first appointment. To shorten the wait, the center has introduced a "single-session" model. Instead of committing to a series of weekly meetings, students can book one 50-minute session that focuses on a specific issue, such as exam anxiety or a conflict with a roommate. If they need more support afterward, they can be referred to regular counseling.

The center has also trained 40 student volunteers as peer listeners. These volunteers do not give professional advice, but they are available in the library every weekday evening to talk with classmates who simply need someone to listen. "Sometimes talking to someone my own age feels less stressful," said Wang Yu-ting, a sophomore in the Department of Chemistry.

Not everyone is satisfied, however. Several graduate students say the center's opening hours do not fit their lab schedules, which often run late into the evening. In response, the center plans to add Saturday morning sessions starting next semester. Director Lin also encourages professors to mention the center's services in class, especially in the weeks before final exams, when stress levels usually rise again.
